steps.action: Cite Terada et al.'s Okada-model inversion of eight tiltmeters, which gave crack opening, closing and volume changes for the eruption.
steps.quote: The volume changes associated with the eruption were estimated from eight tiltmeters

steps.action: Cite Yamada et al.'s VLP waveform inversion (0.02–0.1 Hz) of broadband records, which gave an opening crack and an inclined cylinder mechanism.
steps.quote: They estimated an opening crack at a depth of 700 m beneath Kagamiike-kita crater

steps.action: Pose the question of the source mechanism of the ultra-long-period signal, to be estimated by waveform inversion of broadband and tilt records.
steps.quote: However, the source mechanism of the ULP signal has yet to be investigated.

steps.action: Use the live 2018 eruption as recorded by broadband seismometers and borehole tiltmeters at three V-net stations 4–6 km from the craters.
steps.quote: recorded by broadband seismometers (with a natural period of 240 s) and borehole tiltmeters installed at three stations

steps.action: Describe the raw and low-pass-filtered waveforms: low-frequency motion peaking before the eruption, and a dominant period over 200 s that marks a ULP event.
steps.quote: The dominant period of the waveforms during the event exceeds 200 s, indicating that it was a ULP event.

steps.action: Note that the horizontal seismometer components respond to tilt beyond the natural period, and check site amplification against a teleseismic event, finding no need to normalize.
steps.quote: The waveforms of teleseismic event that occurred in Alaska (M 7.9) did not reveal any significant amplitude differences

steps.action: Design the inversion: assume a tensile crack source to cut free parameters (Nakano & Kumagai); use the Maeda et al. (2011) inversion including tilt; grid-search location and orientation by RMS residual; compute finite-difference Green's functions with 3D topography and a homogeneous medium.
steps.quote: Here, a tensile crack source is assumed, because it is the most commonly estimated source mechanism for VLP events at volcanoes

steps.action: Plan four data combinations (seismometers only or with tiltmeters, each with and without the anomalous N.KSHV NS component), because the cause of its time lag is unknown and the best data set is unclear.
steps.quote: we performed the waveform inversion using the following four combinations of data

steps.action: Run the grid-search inversion on the nine-component seismometer data set, which yields candidates (a), (b) and (c) with similar residuals.
steps.quote: Three candidate source locations with similar residual values, labeled (a), (b), and (c) in Fig. 5

steps.action: Repeat the inversion with the 8-, 15- and 14-component data sets; this yields different candidates (d) to (k), so the location and orientation are not unique across data choices.
steps.quote: obtained from the waveform inversion using eight traces (excluding the NS component at N.KSHV

steps.action: Estimate source time functions for all 11 candidates: rapid inflation starting about 2 min before the eruption, then slow deflation from 5.7–15.3 s before onset, with moments of 1.56e15–1.89e16 N m.
steps.quote: They show rapid inflation followed by slow deflation of the crack.

steps.action: Treat the 11 non-unique candidate sources as rival source locations to be weighed.
steps.quote: Here, we discuss the likelihood of each source location.

steps.action: Exclude candidates (b), (c), (f), (k), (h) and (a) using published craters, fumaroles, hot springs, hypocenters, the resistivity structure (C2 conductor), Terada et al.'s tilt records, and the narrow residual region around (a).
steps.quote: Therefore, candidates (b), (c), (f), and (k) are considered to be unlikely source locations.

steps.action: Convert the maximum moments of the remaining candidates to volume change and crack dimensions, assuming W/L = 0.7 and L/Δd = 3000 from published crack and dike ratios.
steps.quote: We estimated the sizes of the tensile cracks for these candidates.

steps.action: Exclude (i) and (j) because their cracks are too large for their shallow depths, and (e) because its north-dipping crack does not connect easily to the vents.
steps.quote: Therefore, candidates (i) and (j) are unlikely.

steps.action: Keep (d) and (g), N–S-opening sub-vertical cracks near the vents with good waveform fits; argue that broad low-residual regions mark reliable solutions, and name this crack the most likely source.
steps.quote: there is no difficulty in considering candidates (d) and (g) as viable sources.

steps.action: Compare the kept crack with published solutions: orientation consistent with Terada et al. and Yamada et al.; volume similar to Terada et al. and two orders of magnitude above Yamada et al.
steps.quote: The orientation of this crack is consistent with those estimated by Terada et al. (40) and Yamada et al. (41).

steps.action: Run a second grid search with finer intervals around (d) and (g), with ranges set to cover nodes within 1.05 times the smallest first-search residual.
steps.quote: we conducted a second search with finer grid intervals for candidates (d) and (g)

steps.action: Reject the new candidate (d2), despite its smaller residual, because it has the same drawbacks as (a).
steps.quote: Therefore, candidate (d2) is unlikely.

steps.action: Compare the fine-search candidates (d1) and (g1) with (d) and (g) in waveform fit, source time function and crack size, and find no significant differences.
steps.quote: were similar for the first and second searches.

steps.action: Retain a steeply north-dipping, N–S-opening crack as the source mechanism.
steps.quote: the source mechanism of the phreatic eruption is a steeply dipping northward and N–S-opening crack

steps.action: Propose that the inflation and deflation record fluid migration from the hydrothermal reservoir through the crack to the craters.
steps.quote: may be due to fluid migration from depth to the eruptive craters through the estimated crack during the eruption

steps.action: Estimate the fluid migration velocity from the crack-edge-to-crater distance and the delay between peak moment and eruption onset for (d1) and (g1).
steps.quote: the volcanic fluid may have migrated at a velocity of 49–100 m s−1

steps.action: Compare the velocity with published ballistic-ejecta velocities and post-eruption subsidence, and contrast the solution with Terada et al.'s in data, time windows and station count.
steps.quote: These values are comparable to the initial velocity of the ballistic ejecta

steps.action: Conclude that 9 of 11 candidates are unlikely and that the source is an N–S-opening sub-vertical crack near the craters, possibly carrying fluid at 49–100 m/s.
steps.quote: a suitable source candidate appears to be an N–S-opening sub-vertical crack near the eruptive craters

tree.answer: Yes: a ~240-s ULP seismic and tilt event during the 2018 Motoshirane phreatic eruption
No: the source is a latent crack inferred by waveform inversion
Estimate source location, crack orientation and source time function
11 non-unique candidate sources from grid searches over four data sets
Weakly: candidates fit similarly and are separated by external geological and geophysical data
Found: one live eruption recorded by three monitoring stations
Partly: location changes with data subset; preferred crack stable under a finer grid search
N–S-opening sub-vertical crack near the craters is the most likely source

end.claim: The ULP event is best explained by a rapidly inflating then slowly deflating N–S-opening sub-vertical tensile crack near the eruptive craters, possibly carrying fluid to the surface at 49–100 m/s.

decisive_move.sentence: The tilt-inclusive waveform inversion with grid search over crack location and orientation produced the candidate sources and source time functions on which every later exclusion and the kept claim depend.

gates.evidence: Data came from a standing monitoring network (V-net) and were not acquired under a stated hypothesis (§2.1 ¶1). Candidates could fail waveform fits and consistency with independent data, and several were excluded (§4.1 ¶3–8). However, the kept crack was chosen among non-unique solutions partly by post hoc criteria such as the breadth of the low-residual region (§4.1 ¶10). Nothing was fixed before the data: the data combinations, the 1.05 residual threshold and the exclusion criteria were all set after the waveforms were seen (§2.2 ¶4, §4.2 ¶1).

imports.field: computational physics (absorbing-boundary technique of electromagnetic origin; inference)
imports.item: perfectly matched layers for the finite-difference boundary
frequency-domain least-squares inversion with inverse Fourier transform

novelty_claims.quote: However, the source mechanism of the ULP signal has yet to be investigated.

limits: The paper reports non-uniqueness openly: 11 candidates across four data sets, with only three stations (§3 ¶1, §5 ¶1). Several exclusion criteria are qualitative and post hoc: distance from craters, resistivity, a crack that is 'not easy to connect' to the vents, and residual-region breadth read as reliability (§4.1 ¶3–10). No resolution or uncertainty is given for location, orientation or volume. The velocity sub-claim (49–100 m/s) is an estimate_with_resolution only loosely, resting on the assumed leak geometry (§4.3 ¶1). The inflation volume (~10^5 m³) and the 8–11 s deflation lead are estimate_with_resolution sub-claims that depend on the assumed W/L and L/Δd ratios (§4.1 ¶6). The anomalous N.KSHV NS component is left unexplained (§2.2 ¶4). The acknowledgements mention referees, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Inference: the choice of trace_series is approximate, because the data combinations stand in for varied auxiliaries on one event rather than on independent traces.

disagreements.target: Yamada et al. (2019), VLP waveform inversion
disagreements.support: The ULP-band inversion gives a volume change two orders of magnitude larger, which the authors attribute to slow deformation beyond Yamada et al.'s 50-s upper period.
disagreements.quote: two orders of magnitudes greater than that estimated by Yamada et al. (41)

disagreements.target: Terada et al. (2021), tiltmeter-network crack model
disagreements.support: The authors contrast their data (seismic plus tilt), single time window and fewer stations with Terada et al.'s uniquely constrained tilt solution, and claim a better-constrained transition from expansion to contraction.
disagreements.quote: Third, Terada et al. (40) artificially separated the two-time windows, whereas the time window we used did not separate the phases.
